sky-angles: Hold one finger in front of a distant tree. Can two things in the same direction be far apart?
Imagine a bright distant star lined up with a dim nearby one. What information does direction alone give?
distance-units: Picture light leaving the star and crossing the gap to Earth. Which event starts that travel time?
What quantity do you get when you multiply the speed of light by a time?
flux-luminosity: Imagine collecting light on the same patch of ground as the star gets brighter. Does the patch receive more light or less?
In the flux formula, which quantity is squared? Check whether that quantity changed here.
selection-uncertainty: Imagine a faint star just below the survey's brightness cut. Where would it show up in the catalog?
Point the telescope at a distant star too faint for it to detect. What would an empty reading really tell you?
thermal-spectrum: In the peak-wavelength rule, check which quantity multiplies temperature to give a constant.
Imagine raising the temperature while leaving the peak unchanged. Would their product still satisfy the peak rule?
spectral-lines: What must an atom's electrons be doing to make the particular line you looked for?
A spectral line comes from changes in an atom's electrons. What can affect those electrons while leaving its nucleus intact?
doppler-motion: Sketch the wave crests in front of a source moving toward you. Which direction of motion crowds them together?
Compare the measured wavelength with its rest value. Would zero motion shift the line in this model?
reddening-degeneracy: Dust can dim some wavelengths more than others. Would that move the center of every identified line by one common factor?
What could you learn from the positions of the lines alone, before comparing the strength of different colors?
parallax-distance: Look at your thumb with one eye and then the other. Does a farther thumb appear to jump more or less?
The observing baseline stays fixed. How would the apparent shift compare for two different distances?
magnitudes: Check which way the magnitude scale runs. Then recall that equal steps on it multiply flux.
Equal fluxes in the same band would give what difference in apparent magnitude?
standardizable-sources: Imagine timing two kinds of repeating stars. What measurements would show whether they follow the same brightness rule?
A period measures timing. What could dust still do to the brightness that reaches your detector?
distance-errors: Picture a ruler whose zero mark is misplaced. Would repeating many measurements with that ruler fix the shift?
Try adding the same zero-point shift to every logarithmic brightness reading. What happens to their average?
kepler-mass: Kepler's relation connects period squared to orbit size cubed. Which root will recover the period?
Picture a wider circular orbit around the same mass. How do both the distance to travel and the orbital speed change?
binary-centre: Draw the common center of mass between two equal weights. Where does brightness enter that balance?
Place two equal masses on either side of their shared center. Which one would sit exactly at the center?
transit-rv: Transit depth compares blocked areas. What operation turns an area ratio into a radius ratio?
Picture a larger dark disk passing in front of the same star. Would it hide a larger or smaller fraction?
inclination-limits: Draw a circle on a sheet facing you. Which part of a planet's motion along that circle points toward your eye?
A line-of-sight speed is one part of the orbital speed. How large can one part of a finite speed be?
hydrostatic-support: Draw the pressure forces on opposite faces of a small patch of the shell. Which way does each arrow point?
Heat can affect the pressure on both sides. What difference in the pushes would support the shell?
stellar-equation-state: At the same temperature, compare the number of particles hitting a wall before and after ionization.
Picture the freed electrons and ions moving through the gas. Could they still strike its walls?
stellar-energy: Count the same outward-moving energy as it passes through two larger and larger spheres. Is any new energy added between them?
An inverse-square rule describes what reaches each square meter. What would you measure by adding up the entire shell?
stellar-transport: What would start an overturning flow if photons already carry the energy through a stable layer?
Think about sunlight warming your skin. What can photons deliver?
mass-luminosity: Write the mass ratio as a factor raised to the exponent in the question. How many factors of three are required?
Check whether the supplied luminosity rule uses a square or a cube before multiplying.
hr-diagram: Halve the temperature in the fourth-power term. How much more surface area would restore the same luminosity?
If each patch of a cooler star emits less, would matching the total luminosity require more or less surface?
cluster-ages: Compare the time low-mass and high-mass stars spend using their main fuel. Which group leaves the sequence first?
Imagine taking snapshots of one cluster as it ages. What happens to stars that have exhausted their main fuel?
stellar-inference: If each square meter of a hotter surface shines more brightly, how much surface is needed for the same total light?
Keep the radius fixed for a moment and raise the temperature. Would the total emitted power stay fixed?
fusion-fuel: Think of a fuel tank twice as big feeding a lamp that uses energy four times as fast. How long will it last?
Lifetime divides the available energy by the rate of use. Which direction does a larger rate push the result?
late-burning: The color comes from the surface. Sketch the core separately and ask whether both layers have to expand together.
Compare the energy of a red photon with zero. What stellar layer controls the color seen from outside?
remnant-pathways: Imagine two equally massive stars, one in a close pair. What could its companion change while the star evolves?
Draw a boundary around a star shedding a wind. Where can some of its original mass go?
initial-conditions: Two stars can have the same mass and different mixtures of elements. How might that change the passage of light?
Find what the symbol Z labels in a star's composition. Which material property does it describe?
degenerate-support: Compare an ordinary warm gas with crowded electrons in a white dwarf. What makes pressure in each case?
Follow what happens when many cold electrons try to occupy the same quantum state. Which rule limits them?
white-dwarf: Check the speed assumed for the electrons when the simple radius rule was derived. Does that assumption hold at the limit?
Changing distance units leaves the star the same. Which physical assumption might break down as mass rises?
pulsar-clock: Count how many pulses fit in one minute if the gap between successive pulses grows.
Choose two different pulse periods and take one divided by each. Are the resulting frequencies equal?
black-hole-horizon: A horizon marks a boundary in space. What material around that boundary can actually get hot and shine?
Trace the route a detected photon must take to reach us. Could its starting point lie beyond the point of no return?
interstellar-phases: Use pressure as a product of number density and temperature. What would happen if both factors rose tenfold?
Picture the same number of particles striking the walls harder as they heat up. Would that keep pressure fixed?
gas-cooling: Check the sign of the net energy flow first. Is the gas actually losing heat in this case?
Look at the numerator and denominator separately. Which one changed sign when heating became stronger?
cloud-collapse: The estimate follows a cloud pulled inward by gravity. What might gas pressure or nearby young stars do to that motion?
Compare a dense knot and a thin patch in one real cloud. Would a uniform-sphere estimate describe both identically?
virial-estimate: Check the power on velocity dispersion in the expression for the virial parameter.
Find the velocity term in the fraction. Does faster random motion strengthen the motion side or the gravity side?
galaxy-mass-profile: In the circular-orbit relation, check what power of orbital speed sets the required inward pull.
Imagine a faster orbit at the same radius. Would holding it on that path need a weaker or a stronger gravitational pull?
rotation-unseen-mass: What does an orbit measure about a gravitational pull? Which extra observation would identify what produced it?
List all the mass inside the orbit, including gas. Which part of that list does orbital speed distinguish on its own?
galaxy-evolution: Imagine a few very bright young stars among many dim older ones. Compare the light share with the mass share.
Which conversion would you need to turn the amount of blue light into a mass?
accretion-energy: Picture two equal amounts of infalling matter. Which one can shine more if a smaller fraction of its energy escapes as light?
Write luminosity as the available power times the fraction converted to radiation. Which factor changed?
scale-redshift: Redshift measures the fractional increase relative to the emitted wavelength. What do you add back to get the full wavelength?
Try starting with a one-meter wave and increasing its length by one whole original wavelength.
local-hubble: Think about two nearby galaxies pulling on each other. What local motion could add to the motion from expansion?
Compare the motion of one nearby galaxy with the average motion of galaxies at many distances.
expansion-content: Draw a cube carried along with the expansion. If it contains the same matter but grows bigger, what happens to density?
Double the length, width, and height of a box holding fixed mass. In the density fraction, where does the new volume go?
cosmic-distances: List what is measured to infer luminosity distance. Would timing a photon measure those same things?
Two lengths can both be given in megaparsecs. What measurement defines the particular length being reported?
background-spectrum: As space expands, sketch two successive wave crests moving farther apart. What does that do to a thermal spectrum's peak?
Follow a light wave as its wavelength stretches. What happens to the energy each photon carries?
recombination: Imagine crossing a space with twice as many scattering targets per cubic meter. How far can a photon typically travel between hits?
Find the particles that scatter photons in the formula. Would changing a name change their number?
primordial-elements: For a nuclear collision to build a heavier nucleus, what temperature, density and time does it need?
Think about the heavier elements made in stars today. Which conditions in the early universe changed too quickly?
cosmic-model-tests: Could another model with adjustable settings match the same observation? What would distinguish their predictions?
Imagine two measurements with different error bars. How should those widths affect how you judge the fit?
gravitational-waves: Sound needs particles to bump into one another. What does a gravitational-wave detector measure changing between its mirrors?
Picture detectors far apart with empty space between them and the source. What property of space can change along the way?
particle-messengers: To infer speed from arrival time and distance, which time would you need at the source?
Two messengers can leave different regions of an exploding star. What would establish when each one was released?
lensing-mass: A dark object still has mass. What could happen to light from a bright galaxy behind it?
Look at an image of a background galaxy. Which change in its shape or position could reveal a foreground mass?
dark-sector-evidence: Match the observations separately. Which concerns orbital gravity, and which concerns the history of expansion?
Compare a galaxy's rotation with the rate at which cosmic expansion changes. Which observation is the term describing?
synthetic-star: Imagine a dust screen blocking half the light. Which flux would be entered into the dust-free calculation?
Hold the distance fixed and calculate luminosity with a lower measured flux. Would the product stay the same?
timescale-comparison: Write the two rules next to each other. Which one involves the cube of the orbital radius?
A light ray has farther to go when the radius grows. What happens to its travel time even at fixed light speed?
competing-models: Imagine one calibration shift moving every data point together. Would squaring each individual error capture that shared pattern?
After choosing the model, ask how far the measured points could shift together within their calibration uncertainty.
further-prerequisites: Imagine refining a model that leaves out an important force. What would smaller computational steps tell you about that omission?
Which points on the plot come from the calculation, and what independent measurements could you compare them with?
